row.note: The commentary makes yawm al-din a day of reckoning under the sovereign; Daniel's Aramaic court sits and books open for judgment, adding an apocalyptic courtroom with deeds recorded.
The commentary's resurrection scene has creatures standing before the Sustainer; Revelation shows dead, great and small, standing before the throne as books open and they are judged by their works.
The commentary joins malik, account and due debt; Jesus' kingdom parable begins with a king settling accounts with his servants, embodying sovereign judgment as creditor.
The commentary's debt image reaches a due reckoning; the first servant owes ten thousand talents and cannot pay, making the account's imbalance concrete.
The commentary presents repayment as the day’s governing image; this king instead feels compassion and cancels the servant’s debt, adding mercy as a complication within a royal account.
The commentary links unpaid obligation with judgment; after the servant refuses mercy, the king hands him over until the debt is paid, joining debt collection to punishment.
The commentary's full-weight coin and unyielding balance meet Daniel's verdict on Belshazzar: he is weighed and found deficient as his kingdom ends, making the scale a ruler's judgment.
The commentary hears “straight” in the perfectly balanced coin; Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity, making straight measure a moral test.

The commentary makes the appointed day the settlement of debt; Avot pictures the world as a shop with credit, an open ledger, and collectors exacting payment, an unusually close Jewish accounting image.

The commentary's straight path is also a balance that does not tilt; Kiddushin says a person should view the world as evenly balanced and one commandment can tip it toward merit, turning ethical choice into a decisive measure.

The commentary brings fraudulent weighing beside the day people stand; Amos depicts merchants shrinking the measure and enlarging the shekel, giving the crooked scale a concrete injustice against the poor.

row.basis: no human ransom for a life
row.note: The commentary says no offered equivalent is accepted on that day; the psalm says no person can redeem a brother or give God a ransom for his life, closely specifying the limit of human substitution.

The commentary's root branch describes a death claim changed into blood-price; Torah law forbids taking ransom for a murderer, a concrete legal difference about whether payment can replace the life-for-life claim.
The commentary asks for the straight path and connects it to a balance that will not lean; Isaiah says the righteous one's path is level, adding a biblical image of moral direction made even.

The commentary links the q-w-m root label on “straight” to people rising before God; Psalm 1 says the wicked will not stand in judgment or among the righteous, joining judgment posture to the division of ways.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The commentary prays for the path of the graced and distinguishes it from the astray; the Didache opens by naming two ways, one of life and one of death, giving an early Christian ethical frame for that choice.

The commentary names a straight way, those favored, and those astray; the Community Rule describes humanity divided between spirits and ways of light and darkness until visitation, adding a Second Temple Jewish account of opposed paths and outcomes.
The commentary treats the day as a comprehensive account; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including what is hidden, into judgment, spelling out why no action escapes the reckoning.

The commentary connects q-w-m with resurrection before the Sustainer; Daniel says sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and some to disgrace, supplying both the rising and the divided result.

row.basis: those in tombs hear the voice
row.note: The commentary's standing scene presupposes the dead are raised; Jesus says all in the tombs will hear his voice, adding a summons from the life-giving judge.

The commentary separates the guided from the astray under final judgment; John says those who did good come out to resurrection of life and those who did evil to resurrection of judgment, giving an explicit two-outcome scene.
The commentary has creation stand before the one who sustains all; Paul says all will stand before God's judgment seat, making universal accountability explicit.
The commentary calls the day an event that arrives and links it to rising; Paul says God appointed a day to judge the world through the raised man, joining the fixed day, judgment and resurrection.

row.basis: day of wrath; who can stand?
row.note: The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and links q-w-m to standing; Revelation's terrified rulers ask who can stand on the great day of wrath, joining both details in one scene.

row.basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
row.note: The commentary treats the day as a certain reckoning and Allah's anger as punishment; Paul names a day of wrath when God's righteous judgment is revealed, supplying a close Christian formulation.
The commentary glosses din as account and recompense; Paul says God will repay each according to works, giving the day’s balance a direct ethical rule.
The commentary explains dīn as recompense and equal payment; the psalm says the Lord repays each person according to his deed, matching that account-and-return sense.
The commentary says no one disappears from the day's account; Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each according to his work, joining hidden knowledge with recompense.

The commentary notes the witness whose memory may fail and the blood that can be lost unavenged; after exposing false measures Amos swears God will never forget their deeds, making divine memory answer human evasion.

row.basis: the approaching day of the Lord
row.note: The commentary presents yawm as a severe event that arrives; Zephaniah calls the great day of the Lord near and hastening, adding a prophetic day-of-judgment formula.
The commentary reads divine anger as punitive retribution; Zephaniah describes the day as wrath, distress and ruin, specifying the judgment's felt consequence.

The commentary distinguishes the graced from the angered and astray; Jesus gathers all nations before the enthroned Son of Man and separates people as a shepherd separates sheep and goats, making the division a judgment scene.

The commentary contrasts those under anger with those guided on the favored path; Jesus' judgment ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other, giving the separation its final stakes.
The commentary connects the straight-path root label to resurrection and standing; 4 Ezra says earth and dust will restore those sleeping in them, adding a detailed restoration scene before judgment.

row.basis: Most High revealed at judgment seat
row.note: The commentary presents the day as the sovereign's account; 4 Ezra says the Most High is revealed at the judgment seat, while compassion and patience withdraw, giving the scene an explicitly judicial climax.

The commentary defines the malik branch as one with command and authority; Wisdom says rulers received sovereignty from God, who will examine their works, making earthly rule answerable to the final sovereign.

row.basis: kings stand before the enthroned one
row.note: The commentary places humanity standing before the life-sustainer on the day of account; 1 Enoch says kings and mighty ones stand before the enthroned Elect One, extending the reckoning to earthly rulers.

The commentary develops the exact balance and full-weight coin as an image of judgment; the Testament depicts deeds weighed for a soul, adding a Jewish apocalyptic scene in which moral outcome is literally assessed on scales.

The source commentary explicitly labels ٱلدِّينِ and glosses it as ḥisāb and recompense; Daniel's Aramaic דִּינָא names the court/judgment as it sits. This is a judicial cognate, while the commentary still distinguishes Arabic dīn from deyn debt.
The source labels مَٰلِكِ with root م ل ك and describes its royal command; Isaiah calls YHWH judge, lawgiver and “our king” in one verse, showing the cognate royal term in a judicial setting.

row.basis: Hebrew יום יהוה, “day of the Lord”
row.note: The source commentary labels يَوْمِ and develops it as an arriving judgment event; Zephaniah uses the cognate Hebrew יוֹם in its approaching “day of the Lord,” placing the judgment in a shared Semitic day formula.

The source labels ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ with root ق و م and explicitly connects that family to rising; Psalm 1 uses Hebrew יָקֻמוּ for the wicked not standing in judgment, a cognate standing sense rather than a claim that both words mean “straight.”
The commentary makes the upright path a balance that does not lean; Leviticus commands honest scales, stones and measures, grounding the image in Israel's market law.
The commentary imagines the final measure as a perfectly straight scale; Proverbs says honest balances and weights belong to the Lord, linking fairness in commerce to divine authority.
The commentary's “standing” coin has exact weight and does not tip the scale; Deuteronomy requires a full and just weight, making commercial accuracy a covenant obligation.

The commentary describes a day when deeds are accounted and outcomes differ; the Talmud says books are opened on Rosh Hashanah and distinguishes righteous, wicked and intermediate people, adding a Jewish liturgical calendar for judgment.

row.basis: account on the day of judgment
row.note: The commentary makes dīn an account and repayment; Jesus says people will give an account for careless words on the day of judgment, extending the reckoning to speech.

The commentary says no equivalent can be offered on that day; Jesus asks what a person could give in exchange for life after gaining the world and losing himself, sharpening the limit on substitution.

The commentary distinguishes a due debt from its final repayment; Jesus tells of two debtors unable to repay whom one creditor freely forgives, showing debt as a measure of mercy as well as liability.

The commentary distinguishes the source word dīn from the related deyn debt; Jesus' prayer asks forgiveness of sins while naming those indebted to the speakers, explicitly joining moral fault to debt language.

row.basis: release of debts in the seventh year
row.note: The commentary uses a loan due at its term to illuminate the final account; Deuteronomy commands creditors to release claims at the sabbatical year, adding a Torah practice of debt remission rather than final collection.
The commentary frames judgment as an individual account; Paul says each person will give an account of himself to God, making responsibility personal rather than transferable.

row.basis: account before judge of living and dead
row.note: The commentary's day leaves no one absent from the account; Peter says people will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead, tying accountability to the whole human span.
The commentary glosses din as recompense and anger as punishment; Paul says God repays affliction to those who afflict, making retribution a balancing of harms.
The commentary interprets divine anger as punitive consequence; Paul describes punishment when the Lord Jesus is revealed, placing that consequence at an eschatological appearance.

row.basis: judgment on wage fraud and perjury
row.note: The commentary joins divine judgment with crooked weighing and a witness who might fail; Malachi says God comes near to judge those who oppress wage-earners and swear falsely, making economic and testimonial injustice explicit charges.

The commentary's branch gloss says blood can go to waste if vengeance is not taken; God tells Cain Abel's blood cries from the ground, a contrary image in which murdered blood remains heard even before human vengeance.

The commentary's qisas branch describes a life claim that can be converted to blood-price; Deuteronomy states life for life and forbids pity, supplying the retributive baseline that makes the conversion a meaningful difference.

row.basis: no payment to return from refuge
row.note: The commentary develops substitute payment and blood-price as possible exchanges; Numbers also bars a ransom for a killer to return from refuge before the high priest's death, specifying a second boundary on monetary substitution.

The commentary says a person's offered equivalent cannot settle the final account; Peter says believers were ransomed from futile inherited conduct not with silver or gold, giving a Christian account of redemption whose means differs from a cash equivalent.

The commentary says the balance is not tilted by a substitute offered on judgment day; Peter identifies Christ's precious blood as the ransom price, a Christian atonement reading that locates redemption in another's life rather than the debtor's payment.

The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and says no counter-value is accepted that day; Paul says people justified by Christ's blood will be saved from wrath, a distinct Christian account of how judgment is escaped.
The commentary makes the day of account universal and unavoidable; Hebrews says people die once and after that comes judgment, adding a concise sequence of death and reckoning.

row.basis: Christ bears sins; appears to save
row.note: The commentary says no offered substitute is accepted on the judgment day; Hebrews says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many and will appear to save those awaiting him, setting out a Christian mediating account while placing the offering before the second appearance.

row.basis: buy truth; do not sell it
row.note: The commentary depicts guidance and error as the two sides of a bad trade; Proverbs says to buy truth and not sell it, treating moral knowledge as something whose value must be guarded.

row.basis: exchange glory for what is worthless
row.note: The commentary's source gloss makes guidance and misguidance opposite sides of a failed purchase; Jeremiah says Israel exchanged its glory for what does not profit, giving the bad exchange a covenantal setting.
The commentary describes hidaya and dalala as a failed trade; Paul says people exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshiped the creature, applying exchange language to misdirected worship.

The commentary asks for the straight path and marks out the astray; Jesus contrasts a wide gate and broad way leading to destruction with the narrow way, making moral direction a choice of route and destination.

row.basis: Isaiah's straight way applied to John
row.note: The commentary's prayer is for guidance on a straight path; John identifies the wilderness voice with Isaiah's call to make the Lord's way straight, interpreting the path as preparation for the Lord's arrival through John the Baptist.

The commentary brings a deferred debt into the judgment image; Deuteronomy announces remission at the end of every seven years, supplying the legal timing and social practice behind a debt's due term.

row.basis: erring from the way of truth
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the favored path from those who stray; the wicked in Wisdom's postmortem confession say they wandered from the way of truth, adding a scene where the astray recognize their error after the righteous are vindicated.
The commentary contrasts a straight path with misguidance; the same confession says the wicked wearied themselves on paths of lawlessness, making the failed route a life of chosen conduct.

The commentary links q-w-m with the resurrection before the Sustainer; the tortured martyr says the King of the world will raise those who die for his laws, adding a Jewish resurrection hope grounded in fidelity.

The source commentary labels ٱلدِّينِ and explicitly glosses it as judgment/account; Moses' song uses the Hebrew d-y-n cognate when YHWH judges his people, supporting the judicial sense without equating the Arabic word's full range.

row.basis: vengeance and recompense reserved for a day
row.note: The commentary glosses dīn as recompense and makes the day an arriving event; Moses' song says vengeance and recompense are reserved for the day when the enemy's foot slips, joining both images in one judgment formula.

row.basis: YHWH comes to judge the earth
row.note: The commentary describes the day as an event that arrives and the balance as just measure; the psalm says YHWH comes to judge the world in righteousness, making arrival and equitable judgment one scene.
The commentary joins fraudulent weighing to final accounting; Micah asks whether one can acquit someone who uses wicked scales and deceitful weights, making the crooked balance a matter for judgment.

row.basis: God demands an account for blood
row.note: The commentary's branch gloss says blood may be lost if not avenged; Genesis says God will require an accounting for human blood, adding explicit divine reckoning for bloodshed.

row.basis: blood pollution; only the killer's blood atones
row.note: The commentary's root branch describes a death claim converted to blood-price; Numbers says blood pollutes the land and homicide cannot be atoned for except by the blood of the one who shed it, a specific legal contrast to monetary substitution.

row.basis: righteous people cannot deliver another's life
row.note: The commentary says no one can replace another's liability on the day; Ezekiel says even Noah, Daniel and Job would deliver only themselves, not sons or daughters, specifying the limit on a righteous person's rescue of kin.
The commentary's final account admits no substitute payment; Ezekiel says the son does not bear the father's guilt and the sinner's own soul dies, making responsibility individual.

row.basis: the price of life's redemption is beyond reach
row.note: The commentary develops price, equivalent and full measure, then says a ransom cannot settle the final account; the psalm says life's redemption is too costly and beyond payment, explaining why no human can buy another free.

After saying no person can ransom a brother, the psalmist says God will redeem his life from Sheol; this qualifies the commentary's no-exchange image by locating rescue with God rather than a human payer.

row.basis: dominion given to the humanlike figure
row.note: The commentary makes the day God's sovereign domain; after the court scene, Daniel gives the humanlike figure everlasting dominion and a kingdom, adding a royal succession scene within judgment.

row.basis: the court removes the ruler's dominion
row.note: The commentary defines the malik branch through authority and command; Daniel's court sits to remove the persecuting ruler's dominion, showing judgment as an actual transfer of power.

The commentary's king has a strong hand and the day arrives with repayment; Isaiah says the Lord comes with might, his arm rules, and recompense is with him, meeting sovereignty and repayment in one image.

The commentary links the q-w-m branch to resurrection and people standing before God; Avot says the dead will live again and the living will be judged, an especially compact Jewish formulation of the whole scene.

The commentary notes witness-memory failure and says an offered equivalent is rejected; Avot says the Judge has no forgetting, favoritism or acceptance of bribes and that all is according to reckoning, directly sharpening both details.

row.basis: settle with an accuser before court
row.note: The commentary makes a debt due under judgment its central image; Jesus tells a debtor to settle with his accuser on the way to court before the judge hands him over, adding urgency before a judicial account closes.
The commentary links a full-weight coin to the debt's final settlement; Jesus says the prisoner will not leave until paying the last quadrans, making even a small coin part of complete collection.

row.basis: Son of Man comes and repays each person
row.note: The commentary joins the arriving day, sovereign rule and recompense; Jesus says the Son of Man comes in the Father's glory and repays each according to conduct, a direct Christian formulation of that combined scene.

row.basis: each receives for deeds before Christ's tribunal
row.note: The commentary says the day is an individual account with no one absent; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what they did in the body, specifying personal recompense.

row.basis: sea and death surrender their dead
row.note: The commentary says people cannot be absent from the day of account; Revelation says the sea, Death and Hades give up their dead for judgment, closing imagined routes of disappearance.

The commentary recalls that a victim's kin may forgive and that payment should be gracious; James says judgment is without mercy to one who showed no mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment, linking interpersonal mercy to the final account.

The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and dīn as recompense; Hebrews quotes “vengeance is mine, I will repay” and “the Lord will judge his people” from Deuteronomy to warn its hearers, giving those Hebrew formulas a Christian judgment setting.
The commentary contrasts a straight path with those who stray; Peter says false teachers have left the straight way and followed Balaam's path, giving apostasy a concrete route image.
The commentary asks for guidance on a straight path; Hebrews tells its hearers to make straight paths for their feet so the lame may be healed, turning the path image into communal moral practice.

row.basis: the Son of Man sits on a glorious throne
row.note: The commentary calls the day the sovereign's domain; Jesus' judgment scene opens with the Son of Man coming in glory and sitting on his throne, adding the ruler's enthronement before the separation already described nearby.

row.basis: nations taught to walk in God's paths
row.note: The commentary asks for guidance on the straight path; Micah pictures nations going to Zion to be taught God's ways and walk in his paths, adding a public, communal destination to the prayer for guidance.

row.basis: God judges and arbitrates among nations
row.note: The commentary places the path under the sovereign's judgment; Micah says God judges among peoples and arbitrates for many nations, connecting divine rule to just decisions among communities.

row.basis: the righteous stand before their oppressors
row.note: The commentary connects rising to the final division of people; Wisdom says the righteous will stand with confidence before those who afflicted them, adding a reversal in which the formerly oppressed are vindicated.

row.basis: first judgment question concerns honest business
row.note: The commentary develops debt, exchange and dishonest scales as ethical matters; the Talmud says a person is first asked at judgment whether business was conducted faithfully, bringing commercial honesty directly into the afterlife account.

row.basis: ransom for an ox owner's liability
row.note: The commentary says a life claim can be converted to blood-price and later says no ransom works on the judgment day; Exodus permits a ransom for the owner of a lethal ox, a sharply bounded Torah case that clarifies which kind of liability can be exchanged for payment.

row.basis: unjust rulers are judged for not walking rightly
row.note: The commentary defines the malik branch as command over a community and connects the straight path to right conduct; Wisdom rebukes rulers for not ruling rightly or walking according to God's will, tying royal authority to a path by which it is judged.
